name: River folk
one_line: The flood does the farming: every year the river rises, spreads over the flats and leaves fresh silt, and the bank gives the clay for the pot that keeps the surplus.

needs: a river reach of order 2 or more within 200 m
a flat the flood reaches (or a bank steep enough to terrace), and clay in the bank

staples: the flood crop: grain or tubers on the silt
waterfowl and eggs from the backwaters
nuts and fruit of the bank trees, mussels from the shallows
how: plant the flats as the flood goes down
a weir of stone or stakes across the reach, pointed upstream
a channel from the river to the far plot
terraces where the bank is steep
preserve: grain in lidded clay jars, sealed with resin
storage pits lined with clay above the flood line
fish and tubers dried on racks

fuel.note: coppice poles and the bank's broadleaf wood feed the hearth; brush burns hot and fast and is what the kiln wants; the prairie and steppe river add grass_bundle, the desert river cactus_rib

shelter.form: wattle-and-daub huts on the terrace above the flood line, storage jars under a thatch lean-to, the kiln downwind at the edge

FLOODPLAIN_FOREST.fuel: cottonwood and willow branch, coppice poles
FLOODPLAIN_FOREST.food: the flood crop on the silt, catfish from the weir, pecan and mulberry
FLOODPLAIN_FOREST.shelter: wattle and daub on the natural levee above the flood
FLOODPLAIN_FOREST.palette: silt brown, cottonwood green, cypress rust

TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.fuel: hazel coppice, ash and oak logs
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.food: grain on the flats, trout and eel at the weir, hazelnuts
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.palette: hazel green, thatch gold, red clay

TALLGRASS_PRAIRIE.fuel: cottonwood branch from the gallery wood, grass bundles
TALLGRASS_PRAIRIE.food: maize, beans and squash on the bottoms, catfish
TALLGRASS_PRAIRIE.shelter: earth lodge of poles and sod on the bluff
TALLGRASS_PRAIRIE.palette: bluestem gold, muddy water, black bottom soil

STEPPE.fuel: elm and willow of the ravine, reeds, grass bundles
STEPPE.food: millet on the river flat, pike and carp, waterfowl
STEPPE.shelter: pit house dug into the terrace, roofed with poles and earth

SAVANNA.food: sorghum and millet on the flood flat, catfish and tilapia, fig
SAVANNA.shelter: mud-and-thatch huts on the levee, granary jars up on stones
SAVANNA.palette: red laterite, sorghum bronze, one green river line

TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.fuel: brush and branch from the dry wood
TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.food: maize and squash on the flood flat, river fish, dry-season fruit
TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.palette: dust, red peeling bark, the river's green ribbon

HOT_DESERT.fuel: mesquite and tamarisk brush, cactus rib
HOT_DESERT.food: the flood crop is everything: grain and beans on the silt, date and fig on the bank, fish from the weir
HOT_DESERT.shelter: mud brick on the bank, flat roofs, a channel to the plots
HOT_DESERT.palette: mud-brick tan, green ribbon, bleached sky

knows: cattail and arrowhead: root flour, spring shoots, tinder fluff
willow bark against pain and fever
nettle on the old middens: fibre and soup
water hemlock by the bank, which kills
plantkeeper.teaches_flavour: why nettles stand tall where the old camp was; why the silt flat grows taller than the wood behind it
plantkeeper.teaches_practical: cattail root and shoots in the hungry spring; willow bark chewed for fever; the parsnip-looking thing by the water is hemlock

wants_from_player: brush and dry branch for the kiln

techniques.name: Digging stick
techniques.verb: a fire-hardened stick: dig tubers, plant tubers and seed, cut a channel
techniques.teaches: the first farming tool and the last one anyone needs; the flood is the river's work and the stick is the folk's, which is why the headman gives you this and not the crop: it is the one river verb you can carry anywhere
techniques.unlocks: the player plants seeds, tubers and cuttings, digs tubers, and cuts a channel from a stream to a plot (a plot near water or a channel counts as watered: a rule, not physics)

techniques.name: Flood-plain crop
techniques.verb: plant on the silt as the flood goes down
techniques.teaches: they did not invent farming so much as notice it: seeds dropped by the water came back; every year the river rises, spreads over the flats and leaves fresh silt, fertiliser delivered, so the plot is never worn out
techniques.unlocks: the camp's crop ceiling on any flat the flood reaches; the river's food rung

techniques.name: Pottery
techniques.verb: dig riverbank clay, temper it with sand or shell, coil a pot, fire it in a domed kiln of clay and brush
techniques.teaches: the river's second gift: a bank is a pit of clay, the clay gives the pot, the pot keeps the surplus dry through the flood; storage is the hinge of the ladder, and the kiln hump is what a thousand years leave
techniques.unlocks: storage jars: the camp banks grain; the potter; a pot for the player to carry to a camp that has none

techniques.name: The river weir
techniques.verb: a curve of stones or stakes across the reach, pointed upstream so the current cannot push it over; fish going up or down are held in the pen behind it
techniques.teaches: the coast's fence works in a river too, and stone lasts: the oldest structures people ever made are weirs
techniques.unlocks: the camp's fish_run alongside the crop; the player can build one at a suitable reach

techniques.name: Channel
techniques.verb: cut a ditch from the river to a plot the flood does not reach
techniques.teaches: the flood waters the flats for free; the channel carries the river to the plot that is not flat: the beginning of the canal, and in the ruins, of everything the canal paid for
techniques.unlocks: a plot away from the bank counts as watered; the ditch visibly carries water, no fluid physics

techniques.name: Terracing
techniques.verb: step a steep bank into flats held by walls of stone or turf, so the soil stays and the water walks down
techniques.teaches: where the valley is narrow the flood has no flat to spread on, so the folk make one: the slope becomes steps, each holding its soil and passing its water to the next
techniques.unlocks: crops on a hillside; the crop ceiling in a gorge; terraces gone to bramble read as ridges (ruin)

techniques.name: Coppicing
techniques.verb: cut the riverside willow and hazel to the stump; it throws straight rods again in a year or two, poles in seven
techniques.teaches: a woodlot that is a fuel crop, no clearing; the withies are the weir's fence, the fish trap and the basket, so the same stools feed the fire and the store
techniques.unlocks: a fuel and withy crop the bank regrows; the fix for the restraint rule

techniques.name: Clay lamp
techniques.verb: a fired saucer with a pinched spout; fat or oil in the dish, a twist of rush laid in the spout; lit from the hearth
techniques.teaches: the river gave the pot and the pot gives the light: the same dish lies in every river ruin for five thousand years; where fat is scarce the oil is a crop too (castor on the Nile, sesame in Sumer)
techniques.unlocks: a lamp to set down inside a shelter: dim, hours, will not blow out; the potter makes the dish and the player fills and lights it

ladder: fire on the terrace above the flood line
the flood crop: seeds dropped by the water come back
the pot: grain kept dry through the flood, the hinge
pots go down the road to the coast; salt and shell come back
growth.restraint: the flood renews the field, so the plot is never exhausted; the bank is coppiced for fuel and withies, never cleared; the weir is a fence, not a wall, and the run passes it; the slope is terraced, not stripped
growth.ceiling_hint: a wide flat with a yearly flood reaches the tribal ceiling and, in the ruins, went past it (the mound); a gorge river stays a handful of huts on a terrace

signatures.what: a hump on the bank of red-burnt earth with broken sherds in the turf: where the domed kiln stood
signatures.restore: cleared: the potter builds the new kiln on the old firing floor
signatures.inherits: a kiln floor and a sherd heap: the potter comes sooner

signatures.what: a round pond in the flat that no stream feeds: the clay pit, gone to water
signatures.restore: restored: dug out again for clay
signatures.inherits: clay already found and already dug

signatures.what: ridges stepping a slope under bramble and trees, a flat behind each
signatures.restore: restored: the walls rebuilt, the flats planted
signatures.inherits: the soil the terraces held: a crop on the slope in the first year

signatures.what: a curve of stones across the reach, points upstream, that the low water shows and the flood hides
signatures.restore: restored: the fallen stones lifted back onto the line
signatures.inherits: the weir works from the first low water

signatures.what: the rare big one: a flat-topped hill of earth on the floodplain, too regular to be the river's work, carried up a basket at a time over generations
signatures.restore: restored: the camp clears the trees off it and keeps its fire on top
signatures.inherits: high ground the flood never reaches: the fire stays lit through the inundation

ruin.plants_differ: the silt flat grows lusher than the wood behind it; nettle and dock stand tall on the old middens and house floors; willow gone to many-trunked stools where the coppice was; the pond grows reeds the river does not

aesthetic.silhouette: wattle-and-daub huts on a terrace above the flood line; a domed kiln smoking downwind; jars in rows; a curve of stones in the river
sounds: the kiln's roar on firing day
props: a channel with water in it

real_world.region: Egypt, from the Old Kingdom to 1970
real_world.note: the river rose each summer with silt from the Ethiopian highlands; fields were dyked into basins, flooded, closed about 45 days to soak and drop their silt, then sown in the mud; read on the nilometer and kept for thousands of years until the Aswan High Dam ended the flood in 1970

real_world.analogue: Brewarrina fish traps (Baiame's Ngunnhu), Ngemba Wayilwan people
real_world.region: Barwon River, New South Wales, Australia
real_world.note: 400 m of dry-stone weirs and teardrop pens, their convex walls facing upstream to stand the current; fish herded in at high water and low; reworked for so long that no start date can be given; National Heritage listed 2005

real_world.analogue: Cahokia and the Mississippian mound builders
real_world.region: American Bottom, Mississippi floodplain, Illinois, c. 800–1400 CE
real_world.note: the largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, 10–20,000 people at its peak c. 1050–1150, some 120 earthen mounds; Monks Mound covers 5 ha and stands 30 m; maize on the floodplain fed it: the rung this game does not build, seen only as a hill

real_world.analogue: Xianrendong cave pottery, and the first kilns
real_world.region: Jiangxi, China, c. 20,000–19,000 years ago; Yarim Tepe, Iraq, c. 6000 BCE
real_world.note: the oldest pottery known, made by foragers in the last glacial maximum, its sherds scorched from cooking: the pot came thousands of years before the crop; pots were pit-fired in a trench of fuel until the first true kilns, a chamber round the pots with a stoke hole, passed 900 °C

over 200 primary canals off the Euphrates and 4,000 branch canals feeding some 700 farms, mapped in 2025; the river ran high on its own levees, so water reached the fields by gravity and breaks in the levee spread it over the plain; the land was left when the Euphrates shifted course early in the first millennium BCE

real_world.analogue: Hemudu and Tianluoshan rice on the Yangtze
real_world.region: Yangtze delta, Zhejiang, China, c. 5500–3300 BCE
real_world.note: rice tended with bone hoes on the wet flats south of Hangzhou Bay while it was still becoming domesticated; stilt houses over the wet ground, black pottery, and fishing and acorn gathering alongside the crop
